`bun update` (alias `bun up`) updates every dependency, direct and transitive, to the newest version allowed by the ranges that request it.

`bun dedupe` collapses these onto the smallest set of already-locked versions (preferring newer ones), saves `bun.lock`, and installs.

`bun why` explains why a package is installed in your project by showing the dependency chain that led to it.
`bun info` displays package metadata from the npm registry.

First-time Bun user called it awesome: the built-in server and SQLite meant no dependencies besides Bun itself, which is their favorite way to develop.

User tried Bun several times and liked it much better than Node, but always hit a roadblock and went back to Node. First the crypto module wasn't compatible with Node.js signatures (now fixed), then Playwright refused to work with Bun via Crawlee.
You can use Bun as a package manager only without using it as the runtime. One commenter switched to Bun because the cost of switching is zero.

On native C++ addons: the end result of bun install, like npm install, is a node_modules folder structured the way it needs to be. The commenter believes it can run node-gyp for packages that need it.
Bun has benefits even when not used as a runtime, e.g. as a test runner/lib if you're not doing browser automation. Another user said Playwright worked for them with the latest Bun.
Storybook is another tool that blocked one user from adopting Bun.
Skeptic: Bun doesn't really solve a big problem they have, and it introduces all the problems of being new and less used.
"I tried to run my project with bun - it didn't work so I gave up. Also, there needs to be a compelling reason to switch to a different ecosystem."
A pnpm daily driver noted that npm still lacks a symlink option, while Bun supports symlinks. Their small team uses Bun for one of their servers but wouldn't recommend it yet for everything.
Bun isn't 10x better, so it isn't worth the risky bet of vendor lock-in with a VC-backed company.
Long-term JS pattern: like Yarn, npm eventually adds the better tool's features. You can spend hours migrating to the latest tool or stick with npm/node and get the same benefits eventually.

Bun's improvements are mostly incremental and easy to fold back into Node (e.g. Node now has native SQLite). For servers, this user prefers battle-tested frameworks like Express or Fastify, so switching is hard to justify.

Bun is already pretty fast on Windows, but some install bugs make it crash, possibly tied to an old package-lock or node_modules, or switching between WSL and Windows. Workaround: delete all lock files (bun and npm) and node_modules.
Request on the new isolated installs: make the isolated linker's default behavior 'nohoist', the same as pnpm.
Bun is now one user's first choice, especially for built-in SQLite. They also found a built-in S3 client when writing a quick script to dump data to S3.
Bun's TypeScript shell scripting API (single file, shebang, straightforward DSL, piping) was really nice and ergonomic. The user enjoyed writing utility scripts with it much more than bash.

User runs Bun for many package.json projects but prefers Deno for shell scripting, because Deno lets you pull dependencies via npm:/jsr: import statements. Another commenter noted Bun's auto-install of imports when no node_modules exists.
Migrated small bash scripts to JS with Bun for its simplicity, speed, and out-of-the-box features (DB scripts without external deps). Quite happy with it.
User likes Bun but hesitates to use it in a pnpm monorepo. They fear migrating only to find missing features, such as running specific scripts on specific packages.
